body.heading: Two meanings packed in one word
paragraphs: In Through the Looking-Glass, Humpty Dumpty explains the word slithy as “lithe and slimy”, adding: “You see it's like a portmanteau — there are two meanings packed up into one word.” A portmanteau was a suitcase that opened into two halves, and Carroll borrowed it for blended words.

Once you start looking, blends are everywhere. Brunch packs breakfast and lunch; smog packs smoke and fog; a motel is a motor hotel; and spork, that picnic compromise, is spoon and fork travelling together.

body.heading: Blends that stuck
paragraphs: Some blends become so familiar we forget they were ever new. Bollywood blends Bombay and Hollywood. Brexit, British and exit, went from newspaper shorthand to history books in a few years. Others, like frenemy, survive because they name a feeling nothing else quite covers.
A good blend keeps a recognisable piece of each parent. That is the craft: chop too much away and nobody can unpack your suitcase; chop too little and you just have two words holding hands.

body.heading: Try it: invent a blend
paragraphs: Pick two things you love and pack them together. A cat that naps professionally might be a napetite... or try describing a robot vacuum as a dustbuster's cousin and see what name emerges. The game is to make a blend that a friend can decode without help.
Then reverse it: deal out famous blends — podcast, hangry, glamping, motel — and challenge everyone to unpack the two parents hiding inside each one.

takeaway: A portmanteau word is a suitcase with two meanings inside; the fun is packing one that other people can unpack.
